name: Modula-2
year_note: Wirth wrote a preliminary memo in 1977 and designed the language in 1978–79; Wikipedia dates it to 1978, while Wirth's own HOPL III paper dates the defining report to 1979. The first PDP-11 compiler ran in early 1979, and the Lilith workstations programmed in it arrived at ETH in 1980.
tagline: Pascal's successor for systems programming, built around separately compiled modules with explicit, type-checked imports and exports.
summary: Modula-2 is Niklaus Wirth's successor to Pascal, designed to write all the software of the Lilith personal workstation, from device drivers to applications. Its central idea is the module: a unit of separate compilation split into a definition module (the interface) and an implementation module, with explicit, type-checked imports and exports and opaque types for information hiding. It also added procedure types, coroutines and a SYSTEM module that fences off low-level operations, and fixed Pascal quirks such as the dangling else.
history:
During a 1976–77 sabbatical at Xerox PARC, Wirth used the Alto workstation and the Mesa language, whose type-safe separate compilation convinced him that a Pascal-like language could scale to whole systems. Back at ETH Zurich he simplified Mesa's module machinery into Modula-2, generalising the monitors of his short-lived concurrent language Modula (1975) into modules. A multi-pass compiler for the PDP-11 was working in early 1979, and Modula-2 became the only language of the Lilith workstation that Wirth designed with Richard Ohran, including its Medos-2 operating system; a pilot series of 20 Liliths reached ETH in December 1980.

Wirth's book Programming in Modula-2 (1982; fourth edition 1988) defined the 'PIM' dialects, and Byte devoted its August 1984 issue to the language. Modula-2 found industrial use in embedded and control systems — Delco's Modula-GM engine controllers for General Motors, a Paris Metro control system and the software of Russia's GLONASS navigation satellites — but never matched Pascal's popularity, being perceived, in Wirth's words, as merely an upgrade on Pascal. The ISO standard (ISO/IEC 10514-1, 1996) resolved PIM's ambiguities and added exceptions, module finalisation and a complete I/O library, with optional object-oriented and generic extensions following in 1998.

Wirth's own successor was Oberon (1988), while researchers at DEC and Olivetti extended Modula-2 into Modula-2+ and Modula-3. GNU Modula-2, supporting the PIM2–4 and ISO dialects, was merged into GCC with version 13 in 2023.
innovations: Modules as units of separate compilation with type-checked interfaces (definition and implementation modules) in a Pascal-family language
Opaque types that export an abstract data type while hiding its representation
Explicit import/export lists, with qualified (M.x) and unqualified (FROM M IMPORT x) imports
Procedure types: procedures as storable values with fully checked signatures
Coroutines (NEWPROCESS/TRANSFER) as the single primitive from which libraries build processes and monitors
A SYSTEM pseudo-module that isolates and visibly marks machine-level, type-unsafe operations

typing.notes: Unsafe operations (ADDRESS, WORD, type transfer) must be imported from the SYSTEM pseudo-module, so loopholes are explicit. INTEGER and the unsigned CARDINAL are distinct types.

influenced_by.note: Wirth designed it as a new version of Pascal, correcting its syntax anomalies and adding modules.
Wirth presents opaque types as a realisation of Barbara Liskov's abstract data types (1974), the idea behind CLU.

influenced_by_external.name: Mesa
influenced_by_external.note: Xerox PARC's modular Pascal descendant; Modula-2 is a simplified Mesa with Pascal's appearance.

influenced_by_external.name: Modula
influenced_by_external.note: Wirth's language for concurrent programming; its monitors became Modula-2's modules.

influenced_by_external.name: Monitors (Hoare)
influenced_by_external.note: Wirth chose module notation identical to Hoare's monitor, minus mutual exclusion.

structured-control.note: Every IF, WHILE, FOR, CASE and LOOP closes with END, removing Pascal's dangling else and begin…end pairs; LOOP…EXIT handles mid-loop exits.

block-scope.note: Nested procedures and nested (local) modules with lexical scope.

modules.note: Definition and implementation modules compiled separately with consistency-checked symbol files; local modules; qualified (IMPORT M) and unqualified (FROM M IMPORT x) imports.

abstract-data-types.note: Opaque types declared in a definition module hide their representation (PIM restricts them to pointer-sized types).

coroutines.note: NEWPROCESS/TRANSFER from SYSTEM (PIM) or the COROUTINES module (ISO); Wirth left processes, signals and monitors to library modules built on them.

pointers.note: POINTER TO T with NEW/DISPOSE (via the Storage module); SYSTEM.ADDRESS allows address arithmetic. No garbage collection.

first-class-functions.note: Procedure types let top-level procedures be stored, passed and returned with checked signatures; no anonymous procedures, and nested procedures cannot be assigned.

algebraic-data-types.note: Variant records as in Pascal (variants separated by |); the tag is not enforced.

exceptions.note: PIM has only HALT; ISO 10514-1 added EXCEPT handlers, RETRY and the EXCEPTIONS module.

generics.note: Optional generic extension to the standard, implemented by few compilers.

classes.note: Optional object-oriented extension to the standard, implemented by few compilers (e.g. ADW Modula-2).

inheritance.note: Part of the optional object-oriented extension.

milestones.event: Wirth designs Modula, a small language for concurrent programming
Sabbatical at Xerox PARC: Wirth meets the Alto and Mesa
Defining report and first compiler (PDP-11) completed
First 20 Lilith workstations, programmed entirely in Modula-2, delivered to ETH Zurich
Byte devotes its August issue to Modula-2
PIM fourth edition; Wirth's successor language Oberon
Delco's Modula-GM enters production in GM vehicle control modules
GNU Modula-2 ships as part of GCC 13

trivia: Wirth introduced the unsigned CARDINAL type because 16-bit address arithmetic needed unsigned numbers.
Wirth notes that Modula-2 was used for a Paris Metro control system and for the entire software of a new Russian satellite navigation system.
Modula-GM, Delco Electronics' dialect, was the first high-level language to replace machine code in its engine control units.

hello.notes: InOut is the classic PIM library module; ISO Modula-2 uses STextIO instead. Every imported name is listed explicitly.

factorial.notes: Unlike Pascal, functions return with RETURN, and IF … ELSE … END needs no BEGIN. CARDINAL is Modula-2's unsigned integer type.

fizzbuzz.notes: ELSIF and a single closing END replace Pascal's nested else-if chains; identifiers and keywords are case-sensitive.

higher-order.notes: Procedure types make procedures first-class values (without closures). Open array parameters (ARRAY OF CARDINAL, with HIGH for the last index) fix Pascal's fixed-size array parameters.

shapes.notes: Variant records carry over from Pascal, with variants separated by |. Larger programs would hide Shape behind an opaque type exported from a definition module.

signature.title: Modules: walls around data
signature.notes: A local module shows the idea in one file: only exported names cross the module wall, and the module body runs as an initialiser. In real programs the interface is a separate DEFINITION MODULE (.def) compiled apart from its IMPLEMENTATION MODULE (.mod); PIM2 also required EXPORT QUALIFIED lists there.

toolchains.name: GNU Modula-2 (gm2)
toolchains.notes: plw-modula2 is debian:trixie-slim + gm2. Part of GCC since 13; -fiso, -fpim2 and -fpim3 select other dialects.

runtime.notes: Wirth's ETH compilers (M2M, MacMETH, Lilith) are historical; GCC's front end is the maintained open-source option.
